I give a half-star since I can not give zero. It is just so stupid, so childish and so ignorant that the spectator should feel outraged for being considered such an idiot by the director. The story, the events and the personalities of the characters are just straight up invented by the director, who, for some unreasonable reason, wants to depict Napoleon as a monolithic-face virgin who is unable to maintain a normal conversation with a woman as a normal homo-sapiens-sapiens. Maybe Ridley Scott's great-great-great-great-grandfather was killed in the Battle of Waterloo: this is the only logical explanation. And I am not saying that Napoleon was a Messiah: he had his defects (for example he had some troubles with women as a young man) and made questionable decisions that caused the death of thousands of people. But it is not even close to the depiction of the loser-virgin Napoleon, who could not live without his Josephine (the man literally saw men dying every day and never suffered even a single episode of PTSD). This film could have been a great chance to show the general public the good and the dark sides of a, if not the most, complicated and interesting character in recent history, maybe not in his entire story, but rather (like in the movie Waterloo) the last part of his empire. BUT NO. Ridley Scott had to waste the budget of a small third-world country to create a commercial movie for the general public, who ended up hating this movie since, fortunately for us and unfortunately for Scott, we are not brainless. Ban this movie and burn all its copies. After that, hurry up and go immediately to watch Waterloo (1970). That is a movie which merits a view.

Fare un film di 3 ore sull'intera vita di Napoleone non è un'impresa facile, forse è impossibile; tuttavia ciò non può giustificare il quantitativo gargantuesco di inaccuratezze storiche, che rasentano il ridicolo in alcuni punti (Napoleone all'esecuzione di Maria Antonietta, il fuoco dei cannoni sulle piramidi, le cariche a cavallo guidate da lui...), riducendo uno dei più grandi personaggi della storia a un inetto irascibile senza alcun tipo di visione strategica o carisma (ciò che lo ha reso imperatore in primis), somigliando sospettosamente al bruto dipinto dalla propaganda inglese del tempo; se non fosse che Scott, in un totale delirio antistorico, riesca anche a prendere per il culo le nazioni delle coalizioni (fanteria austriaca che marcia deliberatamente su un enorme lago ghiacciato, inglesi che piazzano cannocchiali su moschetti, duca di Wellington di 60 anni, mamelucchi dipinti come guerrieri altomedievali...). L'unico punto a favore del film è la fotografia di attenta produzione, rovinata da personaggi piatti e superficiali. Sinceramente non basterebbero 10 pagine per scrivere ogni singola critica, il film è una cavolata totale, non perdete tempo perché non è un buon film a prescindere dalle inaccuratezze storiche; se cercate un ottimo film che tratti la figura di Napoleone, guardate Waterloo (1970), caga in testa a questo film in ogni ambito al di fuori della fotografia (comunque ottima per un film del 1970).

I'm a big history buff, and this movie was painful both in historical context, and as a movie. I heard from some people that it was bad, and yeah, it is. I watched the directors cut, it was 3 1/2 hours of wasted time. The story is very inaccurate and focused too much on the least interesting things about Nepoleon's life, like parts of his relationship with his first wife Josephine, even when the battles happened and are shown, there's a time skip and don't get enough screen time. This movie completely omitted many battles, many events, and even many of the politics that Nepoleon took part in, like they omitted The Battle of the Nations, The Pininsular War, the fall of the Holy Roman Empire, which was a big deal at the time because the Holy Roman Empire had existed for a thousand years at that point. Both The Battle of the Nations and The Pininsular War also played a big role in Nepoleon's downfall, and both were some of the bloodiest events in the Nepoleonic Wars. If I go further with the historical inaccuracies, we'd be here all day, but it got so much wrong and even completely made things up. Despite the directors cut being 3 1/2 hours, it isn't enough to cover Nepoleon's life because of how much he did throughout his career as a soldier, general, consult, and emperor. On top of all that, this movie is boring,  like so boring, it made Nepoleon Bonaparte, one of the most interesting military generals in history, boring, that is an accomplishment. The effects were very good, the CGI, practical effects, the costumes were accurate to the time, the sets, the cinematography, and overall production quality was good. This movie cost about $200 million, and the production clearly shows. However the editing can at times be jarring, even the directors cut. The score was good, I really liked some of the tracks. Oh god, the acting was bad. Joaquin Phoenix was a horrible choice for Nepoleon, his acting didn't have the chops and he had some weird line deliveries. Everyone else was boring and dull, the only exception was Vanessa Kirby as Josephine, she looked and acted like she was trying, it wasn't much but she had the best proformance in the movie. In conclusion, Ridley Scott's Nepoleon is a god awful biopic, it doesn't cover everything about the titular historical figure, and what it does show is overshadowed by the inaccuracies and the fact that it's boring. The cherry on top was Ridley Scott's response to the criticisms from historians, he literally said and I quote "Were you there? No. So, shut the fuck up!" He wasn't there either, so what's he talking about? When French critics called the movie anti-french propaganda, which it kinda is, Scott said that the French hate themselves. What an asshole! If you are a history buff, don't watch this movie. 2/10

Nothing is even mentioned of all the political, social, and economic reform that helped Napoleon be remembered as a great leader. Instead the decision is made to focus purely on Napoleon’s relationship with his first wife, repeatedly depicting him as a creepy, emasculated, and infantilized weirdo throughout the endless pointless scenes of them together. I was so excited when I saw the trailer for this, since It would’ve been so easy to take this cast and budget and produce an epic period piece on Napoleon. ‘ France… Army… Joséphine .’ These are widely cited as the final words of Napoleon Bonaparte, encapsulating the three most important things that drove his 51 years of life. Ridley Scott’s 2023 Epic Historical Drama Napoleon feels like the culmination of two centuries of British propaganda; which reduces one of history’s most complex figures into a bumbling, pathetic character who’s only drive is his love for his wife to the point it comes off as a total mischaracterisation of the man. Despite my criticism of Napoleon’s characterisation Joaquin Phoenix’s performance is excellent and perfectly captures the character Scott intended to create. The portrayal of Napoleon as an insecure and emotionally immature man who lashes out at those around him and is only driven by having an heir to secure his imperial dynasty left me actively rooting against him at all times and sympathising with Joséphine. Vanessa Kirby’s performance of Joséphine rivals, if not overshadows that of her co-star. She brought a sense of warmth, struggle, and humanity to the screen. This makes Joséphine feel much more compelling than Napoleon and I found myself vividly enjoying her scenes; while having to suppress the fact the on-screen relationship’s historical accuracy is to be debated. Kirby’s performances was one of the only parts of the film I enjoyed as I felt it had decent emotional weight and focus compared to the other parts of the film. Scott’s attempt to encompass 22 years of the film’s namesakes’ life leads to many major moments in his military and political career are rushed through with little to no historical context or reduced to defining moments in the film created to impress and not inform. Moments such as the French Invasion of Egypt serve only to include notable monuments such as the Sphinx and the Giza Pyramids. Additionally, Napoleon’s eventual desertion of the campaign in order to attempt to seize the opportunity to gain power in the shadow of the French Revolution is instead used to further bolster the romance plot that plagues the film. Conflicts such as The Siege of Toulon , The Battle of the Three Emperors , and The Battle of Waterloo excel in being large eye-catching set-pieces with even those who are not interested in military history will find captivating. However, those who are fascinated in military history; myself included will find ourselves yelling at Scott to include what made those battles so important to the magnitude they are still studied today. I applaud Scott for attempting to create a film on one of history’s most fascinating and decisive figures; however the film fails to fulfil what an audience wishes to see in a two hour feature on Napoleon. Viewers wish to see the story of how an outsider from the Corsican gentry who was dismissed due to prejudice, uses the chaos France was in to become an Emperor. The Napoleonic Wars should have been the focal point of this film, however Scott creates an historical epic that is more focused on being a romance with hints of grandiose set-pieces with the intent to appeal to a large audience. Ultimately this leads to a film that appeals to no-one and is instead carried by the historical name associated to it and the performances of Phoenix and Kirby . As many grievances as I have with this film I would still recommend it if you are able to ignore the mischaracterisations and historical gaps. I understand that general audience may be able to ignore these due to not having enough knowledge on the time period or simply not caring, however as someone who’s always been captivated by the time period I simply could not.

critique, Napoléon – Director’s Cut (2023, Ridley Scott) J’avais découvert Napoléon au cinéma en 2023, et honnêtement, je n’avais pas tellement apprécié le moment. J’étais ressorti assez déçu, avec le sentiment que Ridley Scott passait complètement à côté de son sujet. Je viens enfin de voir la Director’s Cut, et je dois reconnaître une chose : je la trouve meilleure que la version sortie en salles. Les scènes supplémentaires apportent enfin un peu plus de respiration au récit, mais surtout elles développent davantage la relation entre Napoléon et Joséphine. C’est probablement ce qui manquait le plus dans la version cinéma. On comprend mieux leur dépendance affective, leurs tensions et la manière dont leur histoire influence le reste du film. Malgré tout, je reste persuadé que ces ajouts ne suffisent pas à transformer le film en grande fresque historique. Mon principal problème reste le même : je n’ai jamais réussi à m’attacher à ce Napoléon. Joaquin Phoenix est un immense acteur, mais ici je trouve que son interprétation ne fonctionne pas totalement sur moi. Le personnage paraît souvent distant, presque passif, et j’ai parfois eu du mal à retrouver le stratège, le chef militaire ou l’homme politique qui a profondément marqué l’histoire de la France et de l’Europe. Politiquement, c’est aussi ce qui me laisse sur ma faim. Napoléon est une figure complexe, à la fois héritier de la Révolution française et fondateur d’un Empire autoritaire. Le film effleure ces contradictions sans vraiment les explorer. J’aurais aimé qu’il s’intéresse davantage à son héritage politique, à ses réformes, à son rapport au pouvoir ou encore à l’impact immense de ses guerres sur l’Europe. Au final, beaucoup de ces enjeux restent en arrière-plan. Je trouve aussi que le récit manque parfois d’équilibre. Certaines batailles sont expédiées alors qu’elles auraient mérité davantage de temps, tandis que d’autres passages s’étirent sans toujours apporter quelque chose au personnage. En revanche, il y a des choses que je ne peux pas lui enlever. Les costumes sont magnifiques. Et surtout, j’ai beaucoup aimé la photographie. C’est assez paradoxal parce que je n’aime pas particulièrement le film, mais certaines images sont vraiment superbes. Ridley Scott conserve ce talent pour composer des cadres élégants et donner une véritable ampleur à certaines séquences. Visuellement, il y a plusieurs plans qui resteront gravés dans ma mémoire. Les batailles possèdent également une vraie puissance de mise en scène. Même si elles ne sont pas toutes développées comme je l’aurais souhaité, Scott reste un immense réalisateur lorsqu’il s’agit de filmer le chaos, les mouvements de troupes et la violence de la guerre. Au final, cette Director’s Cut améliore clairement le film. Mais pour moi, elle ne règle pas ses principaux problèmes. Je continue de penser que Napoléon est l’un des films les plus faibles de la filmographie de Ridley Scott. Quand on connaît ce qu’il est capable de faire avec Alien, Blade Runner, Thelma & Louise, Gladiator, Kingdom of Heaven ou The Last Duel, j’attendais beaucoup plus d’un personnage aussi fascinant que Napoléon Bonaparte. Je suis heureux d’avoir revu cette nouvelle version. Mais je ne pense pas que j’y reviendrai une troisième fois.

I had sensed that I likely wouldn't be watching Napoleon twice, so I decided to watch the Director's Cut straightaway. What can I say, three stars just would have felt too generous for how completely uninvested I was after the first two hours and before Waterloo came. There is certainly merit in seeing this production staged at such an epic scale, and quite a bit of Napoleon is striking to look at in terms of what's on screen, but not in terms of how it looks. Overall, everything here just looks too clean, too digital and intangible for the battle images to move me in any meaningful way, even though they deserve to be praised from the position of technical accomplishment. By the dialogue and Joaquín Phoenix's performance you can certainly tell that Scott's film is openly mocking Napoleon the man, and making you question how a whole country could have been so enamored with him, but looking at today's tyrants and others in history they somehow always manage to sway considerable masses for their greedy and cruel purposes. Begrudgingly, the film also shows Napoleon's military successes, but still finds ways to show him either weak in them or cruel like in the battle of Austerlitz, and certainly singling out the losses his side sustained as ever increasing and ever more disastrous. A really exhausting watch and a far cry from Scott's own similar output.

Like Napoleon’s march on Russia, the concept was more compelling than the execution - a grand undertaking that becomes a slow punishing slog, reaching the destination only to find nothing there and then sadly limping home feeling cuckolded. Ridley likes to yell at modern critics about historical inaccuracies, which is fair, but he also suffers from modern issues, mostly with attention span problems. There's a reason why his best recent firm is The Last Duel which only focuses on one tiny incident. Everything else keeps expanding outward in search of epic scale, but nothing binds the sprawl together. The only theme here is dourness - on every face, in every room, even baked into the lighting. He turns grand French customs into something administrative and shots battle scenes in blinding snowstorms and fog. Joaquin’s Napoleon, probably needs to be de-aged but either way, is utterly bereft of charm, competence, magnetism, or any other quality that might explain why anyone - especially a nation of post-Revolutionary Frenchmen - would follow him. Vanessa Kirby’s Joséphine is somehow just as lifeless in all her scenes as she is in the deliberately awkward sex scenes. Their relationship is supposed to be his driving force, but all we get is one narrated letter from her to him. By the end, the central mystery isn’t the man, the myth, the legend - that remains better served by 20 minute YouTube videos. The mystery is why this movie needed to exist. Five stars if Ridley had redirected his energies toward making Gladiator II better.

Abba sung about Waterloo in under 3 minutes whereas, for Ridley Scott, his tale of that particular battle, and the life of Napoleon, is closer to 3 hours with an even longer, supposedly 4-hour version coming to AppleTV+. Enough with the facetiousness, Scott’s film of this titanic (but, ironically, pint-sized) figure unfortunately isn’t quite the definite article. Cramming the life of the Emperor, his myriad battles and the ongoing political circumstances, both in France and Europe at the time, into one film was always going to incur a long and unwieldy runtime. Scott does pretty well to keep proceedings clear and moving forward briskly but, because of this approach, a few spots of the history get muddled and you’re left with an interesting and broad overview, albeit one lacking true depth. Scott’s focus is more on the man himself and it works as a character study. On equal footing with the fighting is Napoleon’s relationship with his wife Josephine and it is in these scenes that we get our true glimpse into the man and the true brilliance of Joaquin Phoenix’s portrayal (excellent, as always, and bound to be awards-nominated.) Phoenix tows the line perfectly between showing the stern stoicism of the commander and the vulnerable insecurities of the man. It’s an unbiased and honest portrayal and it’s interesting to speculate and delve beyond just a timeline of events. However, despite attempts to lighten the mood at points with a spot of humour or an original take on the period drama concept, it suffers a little from fustiness and those bright spots only serve to show what this film potentially could have been under different circumstances. It feels like it can’t quite decide what to be and this scattershot nature lets it down. Those more speculative, intimate scenes of Napoleon and Josephine therefore stand as the film’s heart, beyond the wider historical context and scenes of war. It’s also, sadly, very difficult to follow what’s going on in those battle sequences. Great credit must go to all involved for staging such grand scenes but, unfortunately, all bar one suffer from some sort of debilitating factor: too dark, too fast in the edit, too confusing. The Battle of Austerlitz is the one true triumph here and is a sequence to place up there with cinematic large-scale battle scenes. It’s another example where the film shows what it could have been, only fuelling the frustration further. Sadly, Napoleon is just a teensy bit stale and a teensy bit boring. Too unforgivable adjectives in a film of this scale and with a figure of this much interest and importance at its centre (and also from the director of Gladiator.) Hopefully, the longer cut will prove to be the one but a little Swedish-pop, Midas-touch originality is needed here. ⭐️⭐️⭐️

No tanto por el conquistador, sino por el hombre. Siempre he sentido una extraña conexión con esa faceta suya que buscaba desesperadamente ser amado. Podrá sonar absurdo, pero mientras más leo sobre él, más entiendo que detrás del uniforme había alguien tan brillante como vulnerable. La película, con todos sus defectos —que son demasiados—, logra mostrar precisamente eso. No al estratega que puso de rodillas a media Europa, sino al hombre que parecía invencible en el campo de batalla y completamente indefenso frente al amor. Esa contradicción fue, para mí, lo más interesante del filme. Le sumo media estrella únicamente por esa representación. Porque, aunque la ejecución sea irregular, consiguió recordarme que Napoleón conquistó reinos enteros, pero jamás logró conquistar aquello que más deseaba. Hay algo profundamente trágico en morir siendo una leyenda y seguir sintiendo que el amor siempre te quedó demasiado lejos. Ahora bien, como película histórica deja mucho que desear. Hay errores difíciles de ignorar: el supuesto bombardeo a las pirámides de Guiza, la forma en que muestran a Napoleón liderando cargas de caballería o el encuentro cara a cara con Wellington, algo que nunca ocurrió. Aun así, me quedo con esa imagen del emperador derrotado no por un ejército, sino por sus propias carencias emocionales. Paradójicamente, esa fue la batalla que nunca pudo ganar. P.D Algo curioso. Seppur la director's cut non scomodi mai realmente la parola noia, ci troviamo di fronte ad una visione deliberatamente impegnativa, anche grazie ad una struttura narrativa ambiziosa che nel dilungarsi in alcune (spettacolari) sequenze sembra arrivare ai titoli di coda visibilmente stanca. -La mancanza di una soddisfacente lettura militare del protagonista. Un'assenza arginata molto bene dalla bravura del suo interprete (che di transalpino, nonostante la premessa fatta, ha veramente poco) ma che cede inevitabilmente di fronte ad una chiave di lettura maggiormente analitica: se sul fronte psicologico la figura di Napoleone Bonaparte, immersa nell'insicurezza e arroganza, è ben leggibile, dispiace non poter dire lo stesso del personaggio quando vediamo quest'ultimo muovere i propri passi nel contesto bellico. Puoi farmelo britannico, egiziano, senegalese, quello che vuoi, ma in un biopic di tale portata sarebbe necessario assaporare l'idea del genio militare e politico che la storia nel tempo ha più volte descritto. Un peccato, visto il comparto scenico e tecnico che abbraccia l'intera pellicola e che rende a dir poco memorabili le battaglie combattute da Napoleone. Alors j’ai revu Napoléon de Ridley Scott, et je dois avouer que, malgré ce que j’avais dit dans ma précédente review, le film n’est pas catastrophique, loin de là. En fait, il est assez incompris, et au final pas si mal. En fait, l’erreur que j’avais commise à été de voir le film en salle, et non de voir la director’s cut, qui rajoute une cinquantaine de minutes au film. Si bien que ces problèmes de montage, de transitions, de lien entre les scènes, sont réglés en voyant la version finale. Ici, malgré quelques défauts qui persistent, tout est assez bien rythmé, bien filmé, si on évite les scènes de batailles qui sont le vrai point noir du film. Mais la ou mon point de vue a changé d’un vissionnage à un autre, c’est quand j’ai compris ce que Ridley Scott voulait faire avec ce film, et donc ce qu’il raconte réellement. En fait, Napoléon n’est pas un film sur la vision des français ou des anglais sur l’empereur, ni sur la vision réelle, historique, de ce personnages si ambigu et particulier, ni même de la vision de Scott sur Napoléon. En fait, ce film parle de la vision de Napoléon sur lui-meme, et ça, c’est très fort. Napoléon, dans le film, se raconte tout le temps, invente des histoire et s’invente des vies pour se prouver à lui même qu’il appartient à l’histoire, alors qu’il n’est au final qu’un grain de poussière dans l’existence. J’ai compris ça quand je me suis intéressé aux tableaux propagandistes de Jaques Louis David, qui sont repris dans le film. Mais, et c’est ce qui est intéressant, c’est que Scott montre l’avant et l’après du tableau, pour deconstruire le mythe et prouver à tout le monde la fraude qu’est Napoléon, qui a essayer de s’imiscer dans une histoire dont il n’aurait jamais du faire partie. Bref, une proposition très intéressante et très bien mise en scène, qui m’à fait évoluer et modifier mon appréciation de ce film. On est loin du niveau de Gance, mais ça reste un bon film, malgré quelques défauts.

Director’s Cut I have really mixed feelings on this. While I have to say this is an outstanding production with stellar cinematography, amazing set and costume design and superb sound. The biggest issue for me was its uneven tone which treated the war time events with a dramatic seriousness, while the parts that focused on Napoleon’s personal life felt satirical. I have no idea whether this was intentional or not but it really threw me off. I also wasn’t the biggest fan of Joaquin Phoenix in this role due to the conflicting tone but I think that’s mostly down to the script which felt like Ridley Scott wanted to present Napoleon as a fragile pathetic character who hid behind his tactical genius, but I just found it to be jarring with it feeling like two separate characters and Phoenix was way too old for the majority of this role. I have heard criticism about the plot being shallow with it feeling like it quickly jumps to and from major plot points. I didn’t really think it did that but I must only presume this is due to the extra depth added within the Directors Cut. The action sequences in this were excellent and really showed Ridley Scott at his best with hard hitting brutality and authentic choreography creating some of the best large scale battles I’ve seen. The ending was also phenomenal. Vanessa Kirby was fantastic as Josephine who played a key role in Napoleon’s story. But, there are a lot of characters in this and while I don’t think anyone was particularly bad no one really stood out to me. I did enjoy this film with the full 3 and half hours feeling generally well paced. For me it doesn’t do much wrong apart from as I said the weird tone surrounding Napoleon but unfortunately that is a big deal considering the whole film surrounds him. This could have been an absolutely incredible film. I would love to know if the awkward portrayal of Napoleon’s personal life was intentional and maybe inspired by England’s historical propaganda that did show him as weak and childish. I would like to watch this again one day knowing what to expect.

Un deuxième visionnage bien rentable, cette fois-ci vu en version intégrale qui rajoute 48 minutes environ. Je me rappelle que la version cinéma de 2h40 donnait l'impression que les évènements s'enchaînaient bêtement et sans raison, ce qui n'est pas le cas dans la director's cut. Napoléon de Ridley Scott est indéniablement imparfait et inégal. La photographie est parfois sublime, parfois absolument infecte. Bien sûr, c'est plus souvent beau que laid... Mais je ne peux vraiment pas passer outre cette scène d'ouverture affreuse, qui annonce vraiment mal le film. Qu'est-ce que c'est moche pendant la première minute ! La musique aussi est pompeuse pendant une bonne heure avant de devenir bonne. Mais les scènes d'action sont particulièrement réussies : très belles, toutes uniques, on comprend bien ce qui s'y passe (pas comme dans un certain blockbuster récent que je ne citerai pas...), et durent globalement le temps qu'il faut. Il faut noter que le film s'essouffle un peu pendant la deuxième heure avant de repartir de plus belle. En terme de mise en scène, c'est à la fois subtil, maîtrisé, et parfois un poil grossier/burlesque, ce qui n'est pas nécessairement un défaut. Je pense que c'est le genre de films ou beaucoup de détails nous échappent et que l'on découvre au fur et à mesure des visionnages. Ensuite évidemment, là où le film ne prend pas tellement de risques en matière de costumes et de décors (ce qui me dérange un peu car la reconstitution historique ne m'intéresse franchement pas, et je n'aime pas tellement le style de cette époque), il en prend énormément sur le fond. Et cette prise de risque fondamentale, qui est de faire de Napoléon un personnage mauvais et comique, est géniale ! Elle porte franchement le film et lui donne un intérêt. Phoenix est excellent dans ce rôle (sous certains angles, la ressemblance avec le vrai Napoléon est frappante). L'idée de faire d'un Empereur que la tradition historique prend au sérieux un simple cocu immature en manque d'amour et qui a clairement des dizaines de manques à combler, c'est merveilleux. De quoi rendre fou tout morveux qui prétend être un patriote en adorant ce neuille de Napoléon. Qu'est-ce que je préfère un protagoniste de la sorte, absolument inattendu et presque dégoûtant, à un personnage historique qui répond simplement aux attentes d'un spectateur lambda qui s'attend à un film épique comme les autres, du style Pierre Niney dans le Comte de Monte-Cristo. Bien entendu, j'aime bien Pierre Niney malgré sa filmo douteuse, mais le comparer à Phoenix c'est comme comparer une panthère et un moustique. Aussi pour revenir sur le personnage de Napoléon, j'apprécie beaucoup l'idée d'en faire un mégalo matrixé par l'envie de devenir un des grands de l'histoire au point d'écrire sa propre histoire de son vivant. (Bien sûr Napoléon de la vraie vie était aussi quelqu'un d'intelligent, à l'origine de plusieurs avancées notables, un fin stratège etc... Ok, mais dans un film c'est pas intéressant de voir ça. Je considère également qu'une grande intuition n'empêche en rien qu'il fut une grosse merde humaine). Les deux motifs sur lesquels je devrai davantage me concentrer au prochain visionnage seront la possessivité de Napoléon à l'égard de Joséphine/La France, et la lumière céleste. Bref, un film imparfait mais pour lequel j'ai étonnement développé avec le temps une réelle tendresse. Inutile de préciser que tout ce qui est vérité ou crédibilité historique est pour moins un non-argument car il s'agit de fiction, et que Ridley Scott a bien raison de se torcher le cul avec les livres d'histoire.

I've always thought that making a film about a great historical figure is one of the hardest things a director can do. Unless it's a TV series or a whole film saga, trying to fit an entire life into a single movie means leaving out a lot of important moments. And when that person is Napoleon Bonaparte—a man whose life was defined by politics, military genius, and an incredibly complex personality—the challenge becomes even greater. Any filmmaker has to balance historical accuracy with cinematic spectacle, and I think Ridley Scott only partially succeeds. The film follows the major milestones of Napoleon's life in chronological order and recreates some of his most famous campaigns. At the same time, it takes several dramatic liberties to make them more visually impressive. The cannon fire aimed at the Pyramids never happened, Napoleon wasn't present at Marie Antoinette's execution, and the famous frozen lake sequence at Austerlitz is a huge exaggeration of what actually took place. Those scenes are entertaining, but they prioritize spectacle over history. Honestly, those changes don't bother me that much because they're based on real events that have simply been dramatized. What I do miss are the omissions that make it harder to understand who Napoleon really was. The film barely touches on his background as a member of the Corsican minor nobility, something that was essential in allowing him to attend military school in France and begin the career that eventually led him to become Emperor. Joséphine also deserved a more nuanced portrayal. The movie mostly reduces her role to Napoleon's wife and his desperate need for an heir. While that was certainly an important part of their relationship, she was also a politically influential figure who navigated the highest circles of French society and played a significant role while Napoleon was away. The film turns a remarkably capable historical figure into little more than a romantic subplot. That said, I do think the movie succeeds in portraying Napoleon as more than just a military genius. We see an awkward, emotionally intense man whose love for Joséphine shapes much of his personal life. Joaquin Phoenix captures that contradiction between the vulnerable individual and the unstoppable conqueror surprisingly well. I also liked how the film hints at Napoleon's admiration for Julius Caesar and Alexander the Great. At times, Scott presents him as someone driven by an almost classical sense of duty—a man convinced that his destiny was to serve France above everything else. Whether intentional or not, that echoes the Roman ideal of devotion to the state and adds another layer to his character.

As one with only a cursory knowledge of French history, this bullet point epic was entertaining yet superficial, and I knew enough to see the many inaccuracies. Phoenix plays Napoleon as a bullish, vain and driven man. Brilliant militarily, yet lacking the graces and patience for politics. Letting emotion carry his decisions. I am inspired to read up on the real story. With an almost 4 hour runtime, I was surprised by what was omitted, and realized at the midway point how little of his motivations, relationships, and character were present. We jump through time and while the battles and grandiose locations are impressive, we learn little about the titular man himself. His relationship with Josephine is also portrayed clumsily. Many accounts detail tender moments between them. He clearly loved her deeply, and the transactional and disdainful way Josephine views their marriage in the film reflects an inaccurate and strangely narrow view of history. Phoenix plays Napoleon with a lack of charm and charisma that also rings false and inaccurate. Scott is a masterful filmmaker, and his talents are on full display here. But the story is threadbare and fumbled. Disappointing.

The French historians are correct that this film gets things wrong. They are wrong that this matters. Ridley Scott is not making a history lesson. He is making a psychological portrait of a man who was genuinely extraordinary and genuinely terrible, and who — crucially — was aware of both facts and found them mutually irrelevant. Joaquin Phoenix plays Napoleon as a man who is always, in every room, calculating the distance between where he is and where he needs to be, and who is only ever truly present when he is next to Josephine or in the middle of a battle. These are, the film suggests, not unrelated facts. The relationship between Napoleon and Joséphine is the film’s central argument: that the man who reorganised Europe was emotionally dependent on a woman who did not particularly want him, and that this dependency both humanised and motivated him. It is a fascinating thesis and Vanessa Kirby delivers it with tremendous coolness. The battle sequences are unambiguously spectacular in the way that only Scott, at his best, can manage. Three stars. The film Ridley Scott wanted to make was four hours long. The film we got is three. We lost an hour of Napoleon, which historically speaking, is fairly on brand.

This cut is so much better than the original. While I was planning to save Ridley Scott’s Napoleon until I reached the next chapter of my director deep dive, the opportunity arose to watch it, so I took it. At three and a half hours, Scott’s director’s cut is a substantial expansion of the theatrical version. It doesn’t quite add the sense of scale I expected from an extra hour of runtime, but that’s easy to forgive when the film delivers on the level that it does. Napoleon certainly has its flaws, and some of them are significant, but in the grand scheme of things, it’s a great time. From the opening sequence, the film radiates a grit that seems to seep off the screen, steadily building throughout the runtime. That escalation culminates in several disturbing scenes of political violence that are incredibly effective. Scott captures the messiness of government, revolution, and monarchy with remarkable clarity, making it easy to understand the absolute chaos of France’s political climate during this period. The director’s cut is far more expansive and patient with its pacing, allowing these elements to breathe and making the atmosphere all the more effective. Much of that atmosphere is still rooted in the relationship between Josephine and Napoleon, just as it was in the original cut. What elevates it here are the expanded plotlines surrounding Napoleon’s rise to power, along with the greater focus given to key political and historical developments. These additions provide the film with far more depth and substance than its theatrical counterpart. My biggest issue with the film, both the director’s cut and the theatrical version, is its use of American accents in place of French ones. It’s a truly baffling decision that repeatedly pulls the viewer out of the film’s otherwise immersive atmosphere. It feels especially strange when you have a Russian character speaking with a Russian accent while a native Frenchman speaks with an American one. It constantly distracted me. I understand why Joaquin Phoenix was cast, he is excellent and perfectly suited to the role in many ways. However, I can’t understand why he doesn’t attempt a French accent at all. While his star power undoubtedly helped the film commercially, the decision to forgo an accent altogether may have avoided certain pitfalls, but it ultimately hurts the film’s authenticity and integrity.
